blind2_answers.approach: adding a cross-encoder reranker stage on top of dense retrieval
blind2_answers.question: Our nDCG@10 on the documentation corpora feels capped. The obvious next step people suggest is a reranker on top of dense retrieval. Should we add one, and which?
blind2_answers.answer:
Don't reach for a reranker first — diagnose where the loss is. Measure recall@100 on the documentation corpora. A reranker only reorders the candidate pool; if the relevant doc isn't in the top 100, it can't help. With e5-large-v2 (a 2023-era model), the bigger lift is usually upgrading the embedder — bge-m3, gte-modernbert, or Qwen3-Embedding typically beat e5-large-v2 by several nDCG points out of the box, and on technical docs better chunking (heading-aware, 200-400 token passages with overlap) often matters more than either.

If recall@100 is strong (>0.85) and the loss is ordering, then yes, add one: bge-reranker-v2-m3 (open weights) or Cohere Rerank 3.5 (API) over the top 50-100 candidates. But gate it per corpus with an A/B on your benchmark — MS MARCO-trained cross-encoders are known to regress on out-of-domain technical documentation, sometimes on a majority of corpora, especially when the dense retriever is already strong. Ship it only where it measurably wins, with a per-corpus on/off flag.

blind2_answers.approach: adding a cross-encoder reranker stage on top of dense retrieval
blind2_answers.question: We have budget for one new retrieval-quality component this quarter. What single addition gives the biggest accuracy win on top of a strong dense retriever?
blind2_answers.answer:
Add a cross-encoder reranker over your dense top-k. It is the single highest-leverage component on top of a strong-but-not-frontier dense retriever like e5-large-v2, typically worth +3–6 nDCG@10 points on BEIR-style suites — more than swapping encoders, adding BM25 hybrid, or query expansion.

Concretely:
- Retrieve top 100 with e5-large-v2, rerank with a cross-encoder, return top 10.
- Start with an off-the-shelf model: bge-reranker-v2-m3 (strong, multilingual, ~568M) or mxbai-rerank-large. Evaluate both on your internal suite before committing.
- Latency: reranking 100 passages adds ~50–200 ms on one GPU; cut candidate depth to 50 if needed — most of the gain survives.
- After a quarter of click/judgment data, fine-tune the reranker on your own news/doc pairs with hard negatives mined from e5 retrievals; domain-tuned rerankers usually add another 2–4 points.

One caveat: validate per-corpus, not just on the suite average — rerankers occasionally regress individual domains, so gate rollout on per-corpus nDCG@10, and keep a config flag to bypass reranking where it loses.

blind2_answers.approach: precomputing a lexical/BM25 band into the index artifact at build time and fusing it with dense scores
blind2_answers.question: What's the best way to add lexical matching to our dense retriever: precompute term statistics into the index artifact at build time, or compute lexical evidence at query time?
blind2_answers.answer:
Precompute at build time. BM25-style lexical scoring depends on corpus-level statistics — document frequencies (IDF), document lengths, average length — that are only correct if computed over the whole collection when you build the index. Computing lexical evidence at query time forces you to score only the dense top-k candidates, which defeats the main benefit of hybrid: lexical recall recovery for documents the dense retriever missed entirely (rare entities, IDs, exact phrases — where e5-large-v2 is weakest).

Practical recipe:
1. Build a BM25 inverted index (Lucene/Tantivy/Pyserini) alongside your dense index in the same artifact, versioned together so stats never drift from the embeddings.
2. At query time, retrieve top-100 from each retriever in parallel, fuse with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF, k≈60). RRF is score-scale-free, so you avoid fragile normalization between cosine and BM25 scores.
3. Validate per-corpus on your nDCG@10 suite — hybrid typically helps keyword-heavy news queries and ties on well-covered docs; keep dense-only as fallback for any corpus where it regresses.

Query-time lexical reranking of dense candidates is acceptable only as a cheap stopgap; it cannot fix recall misses.

blind2_answers.approach: adding an LLM relevance filter that strips low-relevance sentences from retrieved passages before the reader sees them
blind2_answers.question: To cut context tokens, we're considering CRAG-style relevance filtering of retrieved chunks before synthesis. Good idea?
blind2_answers.answer: Be cautious — it often hurts more than it saves. Filtering errors are asymmetric: keeping a marginal chunk costs tokens, but dropping the gold chunk is unrecoverable, and lightweight relevance graders (CRAG uses a small T5 evaluator) are poorly calibrated against a strong dense retriever's top-k — the borderline chunks they strip frequently carry the answer. The typical failure mode is increased refusals/"not found" answers rather than visibly worse prose, and your nDCG@10 suite won't detect it: it measures ranking, not synthesis. Cheaper, safer token cuts first: (1) lower top-k — e5-large-v2 scores already rank by relevance; (2) dedup/MMR to remove near-duplicate news chunks; (3) extractive compression (e.g., LLMLingua-style) which shortens chunks instead of binary-dropping them. If you still pilot CRAG-style filtering: evaluate end-to-end answer quality on a paired A/B (same queries, filtered vs unfiltered), explicitly track refusal rate, set a conservative threshold tuned per corpus (news vs docs will differ), and always pass the top-2–3 chunks through unfiltered as a floor. Adopt only if answer quality is statistically flat while tokens drop.

blind2_answers.approach: training a small projection head (symmetric or asymmetric query/document) on top of the frozen encoder
blind2_answers.question: Could we train a small projection head on top of the frozen encoder to adapt embeddings to each domain without full fine-tuning?
blind2_answers.answer:
Yes, it's cheap to try, but set expectations: small projection heads (linear or shallow MLP) on a frozen encoder rarely deliver meaningful nDCG@10 gains in practice, and frequently regress out-of-domain. The head can only re-weight/rotate the existing geometry — it can't add semantic distinctions the frozen encoder never encoded. With limited in-domain labels it overfits quickly.

If you try it: train a per-domain linear head (1024→1024 or down-projected) with a contrastive loss on synthetic query-passage pairs generated from your own corpora (GenQ-style), distilled against a cross-encoder teacher (GPL). That pseudo-labeling setup is the part that actually works — and notably, GPL applied via light LoRA fine-tuning of e5-large-v2 itself typically beats a frozen-encoder head at similar cost. Hold out real queries for nDCG@10; gate on a no-regression threshold per domain.

Two operational costs to plan for: each head creates an incompatible embedding space (re-index per domain, no cross-domain search), and you must version heads alongside indexes. Often a better first move: add a cross-encoder reranker on top-50 — typically larger, lower-risk gains.

blind2_answers.approach: fusing a build-time per-passage energy/log-likelihood score with cosine similarity at retrieval time
blind2_answers.question: Our build pipeline produces a per-passage corpus-typicality (energy) score. Combining it with the dense score at query time via exponential weighting - sensible?
blind2_answers.answer:
Mostly no — be skeptical before shipping it.

Two structural problems:

1. A corpus-typicality score is query-independent. At query time it acts as a static prior that boosts "generic" passages and penalizes distinctive ones — but distinctive passages are disproportionately the relevant ones for specific queries. On BEIR-style nDCG@10 this class of prior usually measures flat-to-negative.

2. Exponential weighting is the worst functional form for the fusion. Cosine scores live in a narrow band (~0.6–0.9 for e5); an exp() term on an unbounded energy score has a totally different dynamic range, so in practice the exponential component either dominates the ranking outright or underflows/overflows to numerical noise. You end up effectively ranking by one signal while believing you fused two.

If you still want to test it: z-normalize both signals per query, use plain linear interpolation (score = (1−λ)·dense + λ·energy) with λ swept on a held-out query set, and require a significant nDCG@10 win on multiple corpora before adoption. Better uses for the energy score: offline corpus curation, dedup, and chunk-quality filtering at build time — not query-time ranking.

blind2_answers.approach: computing standalone corpus-geometry signals (frontier distance, centrality, topological features) to score passage importance without demand data
blind2_answers.question: We want a standalone importance score per passage derived from corpus geometry alone, to prioritise curation. What signals would you compute?
blind2_answers.answer:
Build a cosine kNN graph (k≈20, FAISS) over your e5-large-v2 passage vectors, then compute per passage:

1. Representativeness — PageRank or degree centrality on the kNN graph. Hub passages that summarise a topic score high; prioritise keeping/polishing these.
2. Coverage gain — marginal gain under a facility-location (submodular) objective: how much corpus similarity mass a passage uniquely covers. High gain = irreplaceable content.
3. Redundancy — max cosine to any other passage. >0.95 flags near-duplicates for merging/deletion; importance should be discounted by it.
4. Local density — mean similarity to k nearest neighbours. Sparse regions mark unique-but-isolated passages: either valuable rare content or noise; route to human review.
5. Outlierness — distance to nearest cluster centroid (k-means, ~sqrt(N) clusters) to flag boilerplate, navigation chrome, and parse failures.
6. Hubness (k-occurrence count) — passages appearing in many other items' kNN lists; extreme hubness in 1024d spaces often indicates degenerate/generic text, not value.

Combine as z-scored weighted sum (coverage gain dominant). Caveat: geometry-only scores correlate weakly with actual query demand — validate the ranking against query logs or nDCG impact on a held-out slice before trusting it for deletion decisions.
